slides.0.title: Course Introduction
slides.0.content:
Sauternes — Bordeaux's most mysterious magic; the golden standard of the world's sweet wines. In this misty southern lowland, every autumn morning's mist and afternoon's golden sun give rise to a fungal miracle called Noble Rot, transforming ordinary grapes into liquid ambrosia of deep gold. Château d'Yquem, the sole 'Premier Cru Supérieur', is revered as the world's greatest sweet wine.

This lesson delves into Sauternes' innermost secrets. We will explore the unique microclimate created by the confluence of the Ciron and Garonne rivers; study how Botrytis cinerea penetrates grape skin, evaporates water and concentrates sugars and acidity; understand the demanding craft of 'tries sélectionnées' (selective botrytis passes); examine the 1855 Sauternes classification and d'Yquem's supreme status; and learn how to taste this 'solidified sunshine' while comparing Sauternes with the other two great botrytis regions of the world.

Learning Objectives

🌫️ Understand the Noble Rot Microclimate Miracle

Grasp how the Ciron's mists and the Garonne's warm currents together create Sauternes' unique climatic conditions

🍄 The Science of Botrytis cinerea

Learn how Botrytis cinerea penetrates grape skin, transpires water and concentrates flavour — the scientific principles

🍇 The Three-Variety Combination

Understand the distinct roles of Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc and Muscadelle in botrytis sweet wines

🏰 Master the 1855 Classification

Understand Sauternes' independent classification system and the historical position of Château d'Yquem as Premier Cru Supérieur

🌍 A Global Botrytis Perspective

Compare the similarities and differences of the world's three great botrytis regions: French Sauternes, German Trockenbeerenauslese, and Hungarian Tokaj

After completing this lesson, you will be able to understand Sauternes' unique value philosophy of 'nature's gift perfected by human craft', and to taste this 'golden miracle' from a professional perspective.
slides.1.title: Chapter 1
slides.1.subtitle: Geography and Microclimate
slides.2.title: Sauternes: The Golden Heartland of Southern Bordeaux
slides.2.courseIntro: Sauternes is located approximately 40 km south of Bordeaux, on the left bank of the Garonne river's marshy plain — the world's most celebrated sweet white wine appellation.
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Southern Bordeaux
slides.2.highlights.0.content: On the left bank of the Garonne, approximately 40 km from the city
slides.2.highlights.1.title: The Twin Rivers
slides.2.highlights.1.content: The Ciron flows into the Garonne, creating a unique microclimate
slides.2.content:
Sauternes and Barsac lie approximately 40 km south of Bordeaux, close to the left bank of the Garonne. This sweet-wine sanctuary, covering a total of around 2,200 hectares, is formed by five villages: Sauternes, Barsac, Fargues, Bommes and Preignac.

🗺️ Location

  • Administrative area: Southern Gironde; southern end of Graves
  • Total area: Sauternes AOC approx. 1,900 ha; Barsac AOC approx. 550 ha
  • Altitude: Low, flat terrain, ranging between 10 and 40 metres above sea level
  • Aspect: Vineyards face south-east, maximising autumn sunshine

🌊 Key Geographic Features

  • Garonne: The major western river, providing warm currents and humidity
  • Ciron: A cold-water tributary originating in the Landes forest, generating the mists that Noble Rot requires
  • Gravel and clay: Mixed soils provide excellent drainage
  • Forest barrier: The Landes pine forest to the south shields against cold winds
slides.2.quiz.question: Which tributary's cold waters flow into the Garonne, generating the morning mists that make Sauternes possible?
slides.2.quiz.explanation: The Ciron is a cold-water tributary originating in the Landes forest. When its cold water meets the warm waters of the Garonne, dense morning mists form in autumn, providing the ideal humidity for Botrytis cinerea spores to germinate.
slides.3.title: The Microclimate Miracle: Morning Mist and Afternoon Golden Sun
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Morning Mist
slides.3.highlights.0.content: The Ciron's cold water creates mists, providing the humidity Noble Rot needs to develop
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Sunny Afternoons
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Autumn sunshine evaporates moisture, accelerating Botrytis action and concentrating the fruit
slides.3.content:
Sauternes' microclimate is the most ingenious natural 'winemaking tool' in the world. Each autumn (September to November), a magical day-night cycle plays out here.

🌙 Morning (6:00–10:00)

The cold waters of the Ciron meet the warm currents of the Garonne, generating dense mists that blanket the entire vineyard. Relative humidity exceeds 90%, creating perfect conditions for Botrytis cinerea spores to germinate.

↓

☀️ Afternoon (12:00–17:00)

Autumn sunshine gradually burns through the mist; temperatures rise to 20–25°C and the mists disperse. The warm, dry afternoon accelerates Botrytis activity while simultaneously preventing harmful grey rot (pourriture grise) and other destructive moulds from developing, ensuring Noble Rot proceeds in a 'noble' rather than a destructive direction.

↓

🍇 The Result: A Perfect Noble Rot Progression

This 'humid–dry' day-night cycle may continue for several weeks, gradually dehydrating and concentrating the grapes while maintaining acid balance — a climatic miracle that only Sauternes can replicate reliably year after year.

⚠️ A Fragile Balance

Noble Rot requires a precise rhythm of temperature and humidity. If autumn rains are excessive or temperatures drop sharply, it can switch to grey rot (destructive mould), ruining the entire batch. This is why Sauternes shows extreme vintage variation — sometimes requiring a complete harvest to be abandoned (as in 1974 and 1992).
slides.3.quiz.question: In the Sauternes microclimate, what is the primary role of the 'morning mist + sunny afternoon' cycle?
slides.3.quiz.options.0: Morning cooling preserves acidity; afternoon warmth promotes ripening
slides.3.quiz.options.1: Morning mist nourishes Botrytis; afternoon sunshine evaporates water and prevents grey rot
slides.3.quiz.options.2: The mist lowers alcohol potential; sunshine raises sugar levels
slides.3.quiz.options.3: The large diurnal range imparts a mineral character
slides.3.quiz.explanation: The essence of the Sauternes microclimate: morning mists from the Ciron provide the high humidity for Botrytis spores to germinate and penetrate the grape skin; sunny, dry afternoons quickly evaporate water, rapidly dehydrating and concentrating the grapes, while high temperatures suppress destructive grey rot — creating the perfect conditions for 'noble' rather than 'harmful' rot.
slides.4.title: Chapter 2
slides.4.subtitle: The Miracle of Noble Rot
slides.5.title: Botrytis cinerea: The Fungus That Turns Grapes to Gold
slides.5.highlights.0.title: Penetrating the Grape Skin
slides.5.highlights.0.content: Fungal hyphae pierce the skin, creating countless microscopic pores
slides.5.highlights.1.title: Transpiration
slides.5.highlights.1.content: Water evaporates through the pores; sugars, acidity and glycerol become highly concentrated
slides.5.content:
Botrytis cinerea, feared as 'grey rot' in most wine regions, transforms into 'Noble Rot' under Sauternes' unique microclimate, performing a precise chemical transformation.

📋 The 4 Key Steps of Noble Rot

1
Spore Attachment

In the morning mists, Botrytis spores settle on the skin of ripe Sémillon grapes and begin germinating hyphae.

2
Skin Penetration

Hyphae pierce the thin grape skin, forming countless microscopic pores on the surface without damaging the flesh cells.

3
Dehydration and Concentration

Afternoon sunshine causes rapid moisture evaporation. A single grape may lose 50–70% of its original weight; the remaining sugars, acidity, glycerol and flavour compounds become highly concentrated.

4
Flavour Transformation

The Noble Rot fungus consumes some of the acidity and produces unique compounds (such as botrycinol and noble rot ketone), imparting Sauternes' characteristic aromas of honey, saffron, dried apricot and ginger — flavours that no other sweet wine technique can replicate.

📊 Composition Changes Before and After Noble Rot
Residual Sugar20–25 g/L (ripe grape)300–500 g/L (post-botrytis)
GlycerolTrace amountsGreatly increased (imparts a silky, oily texture)
Water70–75%30–40% (major dehydration)
slides.5.quiz.question: What is the most critical physical action of Botrytis on the grape?
slides.5.quiz.options.0: Accelerating the conversion of grape sugar to alcohol
slides.5.quiz.options.1: Penetrating the skin to create pores, allowing water to evaporate and concentrating sugars and acidity
slides.5.quiz.options.2: Causing the grape skin to produce more pigment
slides.5.quiz.explanation: The core action of Botrytis cinerea is: after its hyphae penetrate the grape skin, they form countless microscopic pores, through which water evaporates in large quantities. This process causes the grape's sugars, acidity, glycerol and unique flavour compounds to become highly concentrated — the foundation of Sauternes' complexity and ageing potential.
slides.6.title: Chapter 3
slides.6.subtitle: The Three Grape Varieties
slides.7.title: The Perfect Division of Labour Among Three White Varieties
slides.7.highlights.0.title: Sémillon (the lead role)
slides.7.highlights.0.content: The star variety — thin skin makes it the most susceptible to Noble Rot; contributes body and a silky, oily texture
slides.7.highlights.1.title: Sauvignon Blanc (the acid guardian)
slides.7.highlights.1.content: The supporting variety — adds fresh acidity to balance the sweetness
slides.7.content:
Sauternes is a carefully crafted blend of three white grape varieties, each with a distinct role that together create the wine's complex structure.

🍇 Sémillon — The Soul Variety

Proportion70–80% (the principal variety)
Why idealThin skin, most easily penetrated by Botrytis spores
Flavour contributionRich honey, apricot, peach; with age develops beeswax, nuts, saffron
Textural contributionFull body, oily and silky texture; high glycerol gives a smooth, lustrous mouthfeel

🍋 Sauvignon Blanc — Acid Guardian

Proportion20–25% (essential supporting role)
Skin characteristicsThicker skin, Botrytis has more difficulty penetrating; lower infection rate
Flavour contributionFresh aromas of citrus, lime zest, green apple
Textural contributionContributes natural high acidity; balances the sugar; maintains a crisp finish and ageing potential

🌸 Muscadelle — Aromatic Accent

ProportionUnder 5% (used in small quantities)
CharacterAromatic variety with a natural musky (muscat) quality
Flavour contributionImparts floral, musky and jasmine notes; adds aromatic complexity
NoteAn excessive proportion upsets the balance; each estate uses it very sparingly
slides.7.quiz.question: Why is Sémillon the most important variety in Sauternes sweet wine?
slides.7.quiz.options.0: Because it has the highest yields and the lowest cost
slides.7.quiz.options.1: Because its thin skin makes it the most easily penetrated by Botrytis
slides.7.quiz.options.2: Because it contains the most natural sugar
slides.7.quiz.options.3: Because it has the highest acidity, balancing the sweetness
slides.7.quiz.explanation: The reason Sémillon is Sauternes' principal variety (70–80%) is precisely its particularly thin skin, which Botrytis cinerea can easily penetrate, allowing the full dehydration and concentration process to complete. At the same time, Sémillon itself develops complex flavours of honey, beeswax and apricot — perfectly suited to a botrytis sweet wine.
slides.8.title: Chapter 4
slides.8.subtitle: Selective Harvest
slides.9.title: Tries Sélectionnées: The Ultimate in Human Craft
slides.9.highlights.0.title: Multiple Passes Through the Vineyard
slides.9.highlights.0.content: Harvesters must enter and re-enter the vineyard 5 to 11 times across the season
slides.9.highlights.1.title: Berry-by-Berry Selection
slides.9.highlights.1.content: Only berries that have reached the perfect degree of botrytis are picked
slides.9.content:
The Sauternes harvest is the most arduous and expensive hand-labour operation in the wine world. Because Botrytis infection does not proceed uniformly, a single bunch may simultaneously carry perfectly botrytised, partially infected, uninfected and even grey-rotted berries — making successive hand-selection essential.

🔄 The Harvest Process

Pass 1
Late September to early October: the first batch of berries or bunches that have reached the ideal botrytis stage is picked
Passes 2–3
After an interval of several days to a week, the team re-enters to select berries that have subsequently reached the botrytis standard
Passes 4–11
This continues repeatedly; top estates such as d'Yquem may make up to 11 passes, continuing until the November frosts arrive

💰 The Reality of Costs

🧑‍🌾
Extremely labour-intensive

A single hectare of vineyard may require more than 100 person-days of labour throughout the harvest season — over 10 times that of a conventional wine.

📉
Very low yields

The maximum legal yield is only 25 hl/ha (a typical red wine region allows 50–60 hl/ha). At Château d'Yquem, each vine produces on average only one glass of wine (approximately 100 ml).

🌧️
Vintage risk

In unfavourable years (with excessive rain), some batches may be abandoned entirely — or even the entire flagship bottling foregone. D'Yquem did not release its top wine in 1910, 1952, 1964, 1972, 1974, 1992, 2012 and other years.
slides.9.quiz.question: Why does the Sauternes harvest require multiple successive passes through the vineyard (tries sélectionnées)?
slides.9.quiz.options.0: Because the vineyard is too large to pick in one pass
slides.9.quiz.options.1: Because Botrytis infection is not simultaneous — each berry reaches its peak at a different time
slides.9.quiz.options.2: To allow the grapes to receive maximum sun exposure
slides.9.quiz.options.3: Because the workers' physical endurance limits them to working in batches
slides.9.quiz.explanation: The fundamental reason Sauternes must harvest in multiple passes is that Botrytis does not uniformly infect the entire vineyard or even a single bunch. Within the same bunch, one half may be perfectly botrytised while the other half is still uninfected, so the team must re-enter repeatedly, picking only the berries that have reached the ideal stage at that moment. This 'berry-by-berry selection' craft is the core reason for Sauternes' high production cost.
slides.10.title: Chapter 5
slides.10.subtitle: The 1855 Classification
slides.11.title: The 1855 Sauternes Classification: A Unique 'Premier Cru Supérieur'
slides.11.highlights.0.title: Premier Cru Supérieur
slides.11.highlights.0.content: Château d'Yquem — the only sweet wine in the world to hold this grade
slides.11.highlights.1.title: 1ers & 2èmes Crus
slides.11.highlights.1.content: 11 first growths and 15 second growths form the complete classification hierarchy
slides.11.content:
In 1855, Napoleon III simultaneously established the Médoc and Sauternes classifications for the Paris World Exhibition. The Sauternes classification is a separate document, with at its very apex a special tier created for Château d'Yquem alone.

👑 Premier Cru Supérieur (the only estate)

Château d'Yquem — the only sweet wine in the world to hold this grade. An irreplaceable benchmark.

⭐ Premiers Crus (First Growths — 11 estates)

Château La Tour Blanche, Château Lafaurie-Peyraguey, Château Clos Haut-Peyraguey, Château de Rayne Vigneau, Château Suduiraut, Château Coutet (Barsac), Château Climens (Barsac), Château Guiraud, Château Rieussec, Château Rabaud-Promis, Château Sigalas-Rabaud

⭐⭐ Deuxièmes Crus (Second Growths — 15 estates)

Château de Myrat, Château Doisy-Daëne, Château Doisy-Dubroca, Château Doisy-Védrines, Château d'Arche, Château Filhot, Château Broustet, Château Nairac, Château Caillou, Château Suau, Château de Malle, Château Romer, Château Romer du Hayot, Château Lamothe, Château Lamothe Guignard

💡 Sauternes vs. the Médoc Classification: The Sauternes classification has never been revised (the Médoc promoted Mouton Rothschild in 1973); each estate's ranking has remained unchanged for 170 years — an exceptionally stable system.
slides.11.quiz.question: In the 1855 Sauternes classification, which grade was specially created for Château d'Yquem?
slides.11.quiz.explanation: The 1855 classification established 'Premier Cru Supérieur' — a special grade above the standard first growths — for Sauternes. Château d'Yquem is the only estate in the world to hold this honour, a unique design in the entire history of wine classification.
slides.12.title: Château d'Yquem: The Supreme Benchmark of the World's Sweet Wines
slides.12.highlights.0.title: The Sole Premier Cru Supérieur
slides.12.highlights.1.title: The Strictest Quality Standards
slides.12.highlights.1.content: In poor vintages, the estate simply does not release its wine — quality above all
slides.12.content:
Château d'Yquem is not merely Sauternes' highest-ranked estate — it is universally recognised as the absolute pinnacle of sweet white wine. Its history traces back to 1593, and in 1999 it was acquired by the LVMH group, further cementing its prestige.

🏰 Key Facts
  • Area: 113 hectares (approx. 100 hectares under vine)
  • Varieties: Sémillon 80%, Sauvignon Blanc 20%
  • Production: Approximately 80,000–100,000 bottles per year (greatly reduced or abandoned in poor-quality vintages)
  • Oak: 100% new French oak barrels; aged for 18 months or more
🎯 Winemaking Philosophy
  • Passes: Up to 7–11 selective passes, potentially spanning the entire autumn
  • Quality threshold: Rigorously assessed each year; substandard batches downgraded or entirely abandoned
  • Non-production vintages: 1910, 1952, 1964, 1972, 1974, 1992, among others — quality is never compromised
  • One vine, one glass: Each vine produces approximately one glass (100 ml) of wine
🍯 Flavour Profile
  • Young (1–10 years): Lavish honey, apricot, pineapple, mango, vanilla
  • 10–20 years: Saffron, cinnamon, almond, candied orange peel
  • 30 years+: Beeswax, truffle, nuts, toffee — profoundly deep and concentrated as 'liquid gold'
  • Ageing potential: Great vintages can age 50–100 years or more
slides.12.quiz.question: What measure does Château d'Yquem take to ensure that its quality is never compromised by vintage variation?
slides.12.quiz.options.0: It buys grapes from other appellations in large quantities to blend
slides.12.quiz.options.1: In poor vintages it simply does not release its flagship wine — quality over quantity
slides.12.quiz.options.2: It uses modern technology to artificially control sugar levels
slides.12.quiz.options.3: It lowers its harvest standards to increase volume and offset losses
slides.12.quiz.explanation: Château d'Yquem's quality philosophy is 'quality over quantity'. In vintages that do not meet its rigorous standards (such as 1910, 1952, 1992 and others), the estate chooses not to release its flagship wine, or downgrades the grapes entirely. This near-obsessive commitment to quality is the core reason it has maintained its 'Premier Cru Supérieur' status for 170 years.
slides.13.title: The First Growth Portfolio: Stars of Sauternes and Barsac
slides.13.highlights.0.title: Rieussec & Suduiraut
slides.13.highlights.0.content: Widely regarded as the first growths closest to d'Yquem in quality
slides.13.highlights.1.title: Climens & Coutet
slides.13.highlights.1.content: Twin stars of Barsac AOC; a relatively lighter, more refined style
slides.13.content:
Beyond d'Yquem, Sauternes and Barsac boast a group of outstanding first growths, each with a distinctive character, offering different price points and styles.

Château Rieussec

Neighbouring d'Yquem; rich and full style, celebrated for its deep orange peel, beeswax and dried apricot flavours. Owned by the Domaines Barons de Rothschild (Lafite) group.

Château Suduiraut

Celebrated for its luxurious tropical fruit (mango, pineapple) and delicate floral notes; full-bodied and often considered d'Yquem's strongest challenger.

Château Climens (Barsac)

Barsac's finest estate; made almost entirely from Sémillon; relatively light and refined in style, celebrated for its elegant lemon-honey and mineral notes.

Château Coutet (Barsac)

The largest first-growth estate in Barsac; fresh and delicate in style with good acidity; in great vintages releases the ultra-rare prestige cuvée 'Cuvée Madame'.

🌱 Château Guiraud — The Organic Pioneer

The first first-growth within the Sauternes AOC to receive organic certification (AB), demonstrating that biodynamic farming is entirely compatible with top-quality botrytis sweet wine — attracting significant attention from modern consumers.
slides.13.quiz.question: What is the relationship between Barsac AOC and Sauternes AOC?
slides.13.quiz.options.0: Barsac is a sub-appellation of Sauternes and cannot be labelled independently
slides.13.quiz.options.1: The two are entirely separate and the styles have nothing in common
slides.13.quiz.options.2: Barsac estates may choose to label their wines as either 'Barsac AOC' or 'Sauternes AOC'
slides.13.quiz.options.3: Barsac produces only dry white wines
slides.13.quiz.explanation: Barsac is an independent AOC within the southern Sauternes region, and its estates have a special right: they may label their wine 'Barsac AOC' (emphasising its lighter, more refined local character), or alternatively choose to label it 'Sauternes AOC' (trading on the better-known Sauternes name for marketing purposes). In terms of style, Barsac is typically lighter than the main Sauternes zone, with more lemon and mineral character.
slides.14.title: Chapter 6
slides.14.subtitle: Flavour Profile and Ageing Potential
slides.15.title: The Flavour Evolution of Sauternes: The Magic of Time
slides.15.highlights.0.title: Young: A Tropical Fruit Feast
slides.15.highlights.1.title: Aged: A Complex World of Amber
slides.15.content:
The greatness of Sauternes lies in its astonishing ageing potential. Unlike most sweet wines, which are best enjoyed young, a great Sauternes only reveals its fullest vitality after 30 or even 50 years in bottle.

🌱 Young (1–5 years)
🍑 Apricot🍍 Pineapple🍊 Citrus honey🌼 Acacia blossom🍋 Honey-lemon

Palate: sweet, round, acid-sugar balance, fresh fruit dominant

→ The Magic of Time →
🌿 Middle Age (10–20 years)
🥭 Dried mango🍊 Candied orange peel🫚 Almond oil🌶️ Saffron🍂 Autumn spices

Palate: richer and more unctuous; acidity begins to integrate; complexity greatly increased

→ The Magic of Time →
🏆 Mature (30 years+)
🍯 Beeswax🌰 Caramel cashew🪨 Flint mineral🍄 Truffle☕ Toffee-coffee

Palate: like liquid amber — silky-smooth, with a finish that can linger for over a minute

🌡️ Serving Recommendations
  • Serving temperature: 8–12°C (too cold suppresses aromatics; too warm makes it cloying)
  • Glassware: A half-tulip or standard white-wine glass; avoid large Burgundy glasses (which accelerate volatilisation)
  • Pour size: Standard pour 60–75 ml (half a red wine pour) to avoid palate fatigue
  • Decanting: Young wines need no decanting; older vintages may be briefly opened 10 minutes to release aromatics
slides.15.quiz.question: When does the optimal drinking window for top Sauternes (such as d'Yquem) typically begin?
slides.15.quiz.options.1: Within 5 years, to preserve the freshest fruit aromas
slides.15.quiz.options.2: After 10–15 years, allowing flavours to integrate and complexity to develop
slides.15.quiz.options.3: Cannot be opened until at least 50 years have passed
slides.15.quiz.explanation: While young Sauternes (1–5 years) has its own appealing freshness, the golden drinking window for top Sauternes (such as d'Yquem and other first growths) typically only opens properly 10–20 years after release — and great vintages can age comfortably for 30–50 years or more. Patience is the supreme virtue when drinking Sauternes.
slides.16.title: Chapter 7
slides.16.subtitle: The World's Three Great Botrytis Wines
slides.17.title: Global Botrytis Sweet Wines: Sauternes vs. Germany vs. Hungary
slides.17.highlights.0.title: German Trockenbeerenauslese
slides.17.highlights.0.content: TBA — the sweetest of all; residual sugar approaching syrup
slides.17.highlights.1.title: Hungarian Tokaj
slides.17.content:
Botrytis sweet wines are not exclusive to Sauternes. Two other great botrytis regions in the world have each developed entirely different techniques and style systems.

Region
Principal Varieties
Botrytis Technique
Style
🇫🇷France · Sauternes
Sémillon (dominant), Sauvignon Blanc
Multiple selective passes (tries); ferments botrytised and non-botrytised grapes together
Full and rounded; honey-apricot character; acid-sugar balance; ageing potential 30–100 years
🇩🇪Germany · Rheingau / Mosel
Riesling (dominant)
TBA (Trockenbeerenauslese): only fully shrivelled botrytised raisins are harvested
Highest sugar (residual sugar can reach 600 g/L), extremely high acidity, almost impossible to fully ferment, very low alcohol (5–6%)
🇭🇺Hungary · Tokaj
Furmint (dominant)
Botrytised berries (Aszú) added to base wine; sweetness indicated by 'puttonyos' (baskets)
Distinctive oxidative-maturation style; candied orange peel, honey, tobacco; mouthfeel like liquid toffee
🏆 What Makes Sauternes Unique

Among the three great botrytis wines, Sauternes is most distinctive for its 'multiple-pass harvesting' combined with 'three-variety blending'. It also achieves the most harmonious balance of sugar and acidity — which is why d'Yquem has long held its singular position as 'the world's greatest sweet wine'.
slides.17.quiz.question: What is the primary winemaking difference between German Trockenbeerenauslese (TBA) and Sauternes?
slides.17.quiz.options.0: TBA is fermented in stainless steel tanks; Sauternes uses oak barrels
slides.17.quiz.options.1: TBA harvests only fully shrivelled botrytised raisins; Sauternes uses multiple selective passes of whole bunches
slides.17.quiz.options.2: TBA adds sulphur dioxide as a preservative; Sauternes uses none
slides.17.quiz.options.3: TBA is based on red grape varieties; Sauternes uses white grapes
slides.17.quiz.explanation: Germany's Trockenbeerenauslese (TBA, literally 'dried-berry selective harvest') only picks grapes that have already fully shrivelled into raisin-like botrytised berries, producing an extremely concentrated sugar level (residual sugar can exceed 600 g/L) but with correspondingly very low alcohol. Sauternes, by contrast, makes multiple passes (tries), harvesting berries at various stages of botrytis development and blending three varieties to achieve balance.
slides.18.title: Chapter 8
slides.18.subtitle: Food Pairing and Service
slides.19.title: Sauternes Food Pairing: The Twin Philosophies of 'Harmony' and 'Contrast'
slides.19.highlights.0.title: Classic Partner: Foie Gras
slides.19.highlights.0.content: The luscious sweetness of Sauternes cuts through the richness of foie gras — the most iconic traditional Bordeaux pairing
slides.19.highlights.1.title: The Surprise Partner: Blue Cheese
slides.19.highlights.1.content: The saltiness of Roquefort amplifies the sweetness of Sauternes, creating a layered tension
slides.19.content:
Sauternes food pairing follows two great philosophies: 'harmony' (sweet with sweet, rich with rich) and 'contrasting balance' (sweet wine with salty food, creating tension). Both approaches can produce an unforgettable gastronomic experience.

🏆 Classic Pairings

🦆
Foie Gras

Bordeaux's traditional pairing — Sauternes' sweet richness dissolves the concentrated fat of foie gras; together they create an incomparable luxurious mouthfeel. Best with cold terrine or mousse (not seared, which can unbalance the sweet wine).

🧀
Blue Cheese (Roquefort, Gorgonzola)

The sharp saltiness and pungency of blue cheese creates a striking contrast with Sauternes' sweetness — yet they amplify each other. The 'surprise perfect match' most beloved by sommeliers.

🍮
French Desserts (Crème Brûlée, Éclairs)

Choose desserts that are slightly less sweet with a rich dairy character; Sauternes' acidity prevents the overall impression from becoming cloying. Crème brûlée is the traditional first choice.

💡 Modern Creative Pairings

🦐
Lobster and Seafood (gratin or cream sauce)

Sauternes' acidity cuts through the richness of cream sauce; the sweet richness harmonises with the natural sweetness of crustaceans, drawing out the finest flavour of the seafood.

🍛
Asian Cuisine (Thai curry, Cantonese honey-roast duck)

Sauternes' sweet richness complements the heat of spices and the caramelised quality of honey-glazed meats — a growing favourite at high-end restaurants in Japan and Hong Kong.

⚠️ Pairings to Avoid
  • Heavy red meat dishes (steak, rack of lamb) — sweet wine cannot stand up to intensely tannic foods
  • Very sweet butter toffees or caramels — the combined sweetness causes palate fatigue
  • Very sour and spicy dishes — they destroy Sauternes' delicate acid-sugar balance
slides.19.quiz.question: Why is Sauternes considered a 'perfect match' with blue cheese such as Roquefort?
slides.19.quiz.options.0: Both are sweet, mutually reinforcing each other
slides.19.quiz.options.1: The sweet richness of Sauternes and the saltiness and pungency of blue cheese create a contrasting tension that amplifies both
slides.19.quiz.options.2: Both come from France and share the same origin
slides.19.quiz.options.3: The mould in blue cheese is related to the same class as Botrytis
slides.19.quiz.explanation: The Sauternes × blue cheese pairing is the finest example of 'contrast' philosophy in food and wine matching. The intense saltiness and pungency of blue cheese (such as Roquefort) meet the full, sweet richness of Sauternes in the mouth; they pull against each other yet unexpectedly achieve harmony, allowing each to show its best possible character.

slides.20.description: Congratulations on completing your in-depth study of Sauternes botrytis sweet wine! You have now mastered this most distinctive sweet-wine sanctuary in Bordeaux — from the microclimate miracle of Ciron morning mists and afternoon golden sun, to the alchemy of Botrytis cinerea, and the supreme legend of Château d'Yquem: Sauternes is the ultimate union of nature's gift and human craftsmanship at its most refined.
